# Keith Dunstan Archive

> The published works of Keith Dunstan (1925–2013), Australian journalist and
> author, preserved and made freely readable by his literary estate. Licensed
> under Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial–NoDerivatives 4.0
> (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0): quote, share and cite unchanged for non-commercial
> purposes with attribution. Not licensed for AI model training. Full terms:
> https://keithdunstan.org/licence/

## Books

Full catalogue: https://keithdunstan.org/books/

## Articles


- [Bird Watching](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/bird-watching/) — Profiles Melbourne's Bird Observers Club, from a postman-secretary who charms Dutch sea captains to the Land Rover expedition that rediscovered the Eyrean Grasswren, unseen since 1874.
- [The New Image](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-new-image/) — On Melbourne's sudden reputation for permissiveness, from a swimsuit-censorship row at the Australian Swimming Championships to the Moomba Committee's controversial beer garden in the Alexandra Gardens.
- [Football and TV](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/football-and-tv/) — Covers Melbourne's fierce row over the VFL's ban on televising the last quarter of League football, then Victoria's new tallest building, the 24-storey Consolidated Zinc, opening almost unnoticed.
- [No Camels for Swanston Street](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/no-camels-for-swanston-street/) — Mourns the decline of Melbourne's once-riotous Eight Hour Day march into a corporate-sponsored Moomba procession, its circus camels banned, then reports on Sandown Park's star-studded car-racing debut.
- [The New Breed](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-new-breed/) — Previews Pan-American's new Miami-style Southern Cross Hotel rising on the old Eastern Market site, then the Lord Mayor's £770 replacement robes after the old ones, handed down for decades, finally fell apart.
- [The Lash](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-lash/) — A spate of unprovoked gang bashings sparks public calls for the return of the lash, running into Melbourne's ongoing water restrictions and a stake-money spat between the Caulfield and Melbourne Cups.
- [Forbidden City](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/forbidden-city/) — An undercover survey of Melbourne's new strip-tease clubs, comparing the silent, appraising Melbourne audience to Sydney's, before turning to the Richmond Brewery's absorption into Carlton and United on Friday the 13th.
- [To the Spencer Street Station](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/to-the-spencer-street-station/) — Compares the muted arrival of the new Southern Aurora express at Spencer Street with the wild 1883 celebrations when Melbourne and Sydney's rail lines first met at Albury, then covers Victoria's new ban on tattooing minors.
- [Football and M.F.L.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/football-and-mfl/) — Covers the Collingwood Football Club's ceremonial guernsey-presentation dinner for its new season, then the box-office phenomenon of "My Fair Lady"'s second Melbourne season at Her Majesty's Theatre.
- [Rembrandt and Phar Lap](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/rembrandt-and-phar-lap/) — A reluctant Melburnian tourist takes a sightseeing coach tour of his own city, from Ned Kelly's gaol to the National Gallery, and finds Phar Lap draws more attention than the Rembrandt.
- [The Release of John Bryan Kerr](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-release-of-john-bryan-kerr/) — On the eve of his release after 12 years, revisits Melbourne's most sensational murder case, the conviction of the charming, well-connected John Bryan Kerr for the 1949 strangling of Elizabeth Maureen Williams, and the newspaper campaign that fought to reopen it.
- [A Viscount, a Viscount, a Viscount . . .](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-viscount-a-viscount-a-viscount/) — Profiles bandleader Tommy Davidson, Melbourne's leading writer of singing television commercials, from his award-winning Viscount cigarette jingle to a £5500 TV shoot with a 46-piece orchestra.
- [Not Only Serious – Solemn!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/not-only-serious-solemn/) — A blow-by-blow account of Melbourne's raging Age letters-page feud between realist and modernist painters, pitting William Dargie against National Gallery director Eric Westbrook.
- [The Great Bank Robbery](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-great-bank-robbery/) — Investigates Melbourne's record £40,000 bank robbery and the mystery of the thieves' 21 keys, then the Puffing Billy Preservation Society's fight to reopen the narrow-gauge line through the Dandenongs.
- [The Stampede and the Fall-Out Shelter](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-stampede-and-the-fall-out-shelter/) — Follows the new south-eastern freeway's traffic overflow into once-exclusive Toorak, then tours a fully-furnished nuclear fall-out shelter on display at the Building Industry Fair.
- [Wild Life in Suburbia](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/wild-life-in-suburbia/) — A Brotherhood of St Laurence survey of a Melbourne housing estate puts hard numbers on Barry Humphries' Mrs Everage caricature, finding suburban Melburnians were overwhelmingly stay-at-home, TV-watching and incurious.
- [Now They Call Him "Satchmo" Bolte](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/now-they-call-him-satchmo-bolte/) — Traces the Exhibition Building's rise from would-be demolition target to beloved 1963 Trade Fair venue via its riotous 1880s exhibition history, then catches Henry Bolte earning the nickname "Satchmo" over a misquoted Anthony Trollope line about Victorian boasting.
- [Paddy's Market to Luxury Hotel](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/paddys-market-to-luxury-hotel/) — Traces the site of the new £5 million Southern Cross Hotel back through the raucous history of the old Eastern Market, phrenologists, dancing ducks, a fortune-teller called Madame Zinga Lee, and an 1898 murder.
- [Inside Toorak](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/inside-toorak/) — An affectionate dissection of Toorak's century of unrivalled Melbourne snob value, from its jealously small postcode SE2 to its chauffeur-driven Rolls Royces and Tudor-revival Village shops.
- [A Little Red Rented Rowboat](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-little-red-rented-rowboat/) — A tour of Melbourne's National Boat Show, where the speedboat has replaced the car as the new status symbol, headlined by Bob Dyer's near-£4000 shark-fishing cruiser Tennessee IV.
- [Return of Norm and Edna Everage](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/return-of-norm-and-edna-everage/) — Welcomes Barry Humphries home from London for a nine-night Assembly Hall season, recounting his elaborate public pranks, including the "Ashburton Line" breakfast-in-a-carriage stunt and slices of ham hidden in a David Jones bargain sale.
- [Not Just a Beer-Up Club!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/not-just-a-beer-up-club/) — Mourns the demolition of the historic Scotts Hotel as Melbourne's city pubs vanish one by one, then visits the newly formed Beer Appreciation Society of Australia conducting solemn blind tastings at the Kilkenny Inn.
- [The Coal Exchange Rotunda](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-coal-exchange-rotunda/) — Architect Roy Grounds proposes shipping London's condemned Victorian Coal Exchange rotunda 12,000 miles to Melbourne's new Cultural Centre, igniting a row over whether it's a masterpiece or, as one letter-writer put it, "ostentatious Victorian junk."
- [£500 Is a Poodle](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/500-is-a-poodle/) — The three-day, city-wide hunt for Heloise, a runaway pedigree poodle worth £500 sent from Adelaide for breeding, complete with a police search, a "poodle posse," and a televised on-air appeal.
- [A Bowling Alley and a Bidet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-bowling-alley-and-a-bidet/) — A tour through the newly-opened Southern Cross Hotel, Melbourne's first brand-new hotel in decades, from Australia's first hotel bidet to its bowling alley built over a bank.
- [Rough Riding for Five Minutes a Year](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/rough-riding-for-five-minutes-a-year/) — Rides the outback rodeo circuit with Australia's professional rough-riders, from the Myrtleford Rodeo's untamed high-plains bulls to a wild-horse race that leaves one rider knocked cold and refusing all help.
- [St Kilda Rd — or Disneyland Modern](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/st-kilda-rd-or-disneyland-modern/) — Laments the once-grand St Kilda Road's decline into brash "Disneyland Modern" office architecture, then reports on the inaugural meeting of Melbourne's new Noise Abatement Society, modelled on "America's quietest city," Memphis.
- [The Fortress Affair — or SP in the Raw](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-fortress-affair-or-sp-in-the-raw/) — Mines the Post Office Royal Commission's evidence on Victoria's illegal SP bookmakers, from a St Kilda penthouse called "The Fortress" that police had to storm by ledge, to a bookie's electronic betting bunker under a kitchen floor.
- [£7000 for "Divinely Dressed Ladies"](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/7000-for-divinely-dressed-ladies/) — The Victoria Racing Club, alarmed by falling attendances, unveils a £7000 best-dressed-racegoer competition for that year's Melbourne Cup carnival, turning the horses into something close to an afterthought.
- [Kindly Smile from an Aberdeen Angus](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/kindly-smile-from-an-aberdeen-angus/) — A dutiful trudge round the ever-identical Royal Show turns up an unexpected revival, a tug-o'-war contest recalling Melbourne's forgotten 1892 world championship pull and its two legendary twenty-stone anchor men.
- [Among My Souvenirs](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/among-my-souvenirs/) — A wistful post-Grand-Final survey of Melbourne's VFL football obsession, from poodle-sized club sweaters to fans who queued 58 hours outside the MCG, plus a wary eye on soccer's fast-growing crowds at Olympic Park.
- [Liquor and the Silk Trade](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/liquor-and-the-silk-trade/) — Traces Victoria's absurd six o'clock closing laws back to a wartime "state of emergency" that never officially ended, then joins 1200 delegates from the Associated Country Women of the World at their Melbourne conference.
- [Heavens! Changes at Georges?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/heavens-changes-at-georges/) — The staid ladies'-only department store Georges opens a men's-wear department for the first time in 82 years, complete with a private-club atmosphere and £250 vicuna coats.
- [Mr Bolte and the Students](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/mr-bolte-and-the-students/) — Profiles David Hirt, the bearded theological student leading Melbourne University's campaign against the hanging of Robert Tait, and the students' months-long standoff with a dismissive Henry Bolte government.
- ["La Ville de Beauté" (as the French Say)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/la-ville-de-beaute-as-the-french-say/) — Melbourne wins bragging rights as Australia's "Conference City," hosting the World Power Conference's 1000-plus delegates through a whirlwind of interpreters, transistor earphones, and two 1600-guest banquets in the Exhibition Building.
- ["A Wonderful Lot of Drinkin' Men"](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-wonderful-lot-of-drinkin-men/) — Marks the centenary of the first All-England cricket tour of 1861-62 by revisiting its Melbourne Cricket Ground opening, balloon ascent, and lopsided country matches against 22-man local sides.
- [The Cup - Some Bowlers Were Low and Rakish](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-cup-some-bowlers-were-low-and-rakish/) — Reports back from Melbourne Cup day on the results of the VRC's inaugural "fashions, flowers and favorites" festival, including the fashion judges' undercover hunt for the best-dressed racegoer under £30 or £50.
- [NSW–Vic: Is Peaceful Co-Existence Possible?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/nsw-vic-is-peaceful-co-existence-possible/) — A tongue-in-cheek peace plan for the Sydney-Melbourne rivalry, sparked by Melbourne's jetport frustrations and a Senate row over an anti-Melbourne pamphlet, complete with a proposed Bolte-Heffron summit in a railway carriage at Albury.
- [Rediscovering the Yarra](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/rediscovering-the-yarra/) — Previews the Queen's 1963 royal barge voyage up the Yarra to Henley Landing, and the belated riverbank clean-up it has prompted after years of floating trash and half-sunken barges.
- [Epicurean Melbourne](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/epicurean-melbourne/) — A tour of Melbourne's booming and increasingly cosmopolitan restaurant scene, from a Scottish Week haggis ceremony at The Capers and shoes-off sukiyaki at Sukiyaki House to Jimmy Watson's Carlton wine bar and the menu-free nine-course extravagance of the Walnut Tree.
- [An Albert Tucker for 2s. a Mile](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/an-albert-tucker-for-2s-a-mile/) — Tours the newly opened John Batman motor inn, Robin Boyd's design showcase hung with original Nolans and Tuckers, from its £500,000 build cost down to its black-carpeted penthouse suite.
- [Mr Fogarty's Silent Spokesman](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/mr-fogartys-silent-spokesman/) — A pre-Christmas beer bottle shortage forces Melbourne to drink imported Toohey's and West End, unmasking Carlton and United's Reg Fogarty as the ruthless "beer czar" who controls the price and supply of beer across Victoria.
- [A Rug of Abyssinian Monkey Skins](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-rug-of-abyssinian-monkey-skins/) — Visits used-car king Emmanuel Margolin, once Australia's self-styled biggest car dealer, as the credit squeeze forces him to auction his Toorak mansion's zebra hides, matador suit, and 500-monkey-pelt rug.
- [Freedom of Beach](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/freedom-of-beach/) — A survey of Australia's unusually open beaches, contrasting the free run of the Australian coastline with the private, fenced-off beaches of the Italian Riviera, Hawaii and California, and tracing the colonial land law and the Bondi bikini scandals that shaped the public's right to walk the sand.
- [Gather Ye Rosebuds While Ye May](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/gather-ye-rosebuds-while-ye-may/) — A satirical guide to how Victorians spend their summer by the water, from Portsea's status-symbol boat sheds and Harold Holt's earnest spearfishing hobby to Lake Eildon's flotilla of cabin cruisers and Rosebud's vast camping ground.
- [Henry Bolte's Brilliant Duck](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/henry-boltes-brilliant-duck/) — Premier Henry Bolte stands in as a replacement batsman in a Centenary of International Cricket replay match at the MCG, kitted out in a garish spotted shirt and a learner's L-plate pinned to his back.
- [Senator Kennelly and the Monster](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/senator-kennelly-and-the-monster/) — Albert Park Lake's decade-long infestation of Canadian waterweed defeats every remedy the Albert Park Trust's chairman, Senator Pat Kennelly, throws at it, from an imported weed-cutting boat to a fleet of speedboats dumping tons of copper sulphate.
- [Under the King Street Bridge](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/under-the-king-street-bridge/) — Profiles Whelan the Wrecker, the Melbourne demolition firm founded in 1891 by a bowler-hatted Irish immigrant, now engaged to dismantle three cracked spans of King's Bridge and busily expanding into wrecking Sydney as well.
- [Mayhem, Rapine and Sin](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/mayhem-rapine-and-sin/) — A gleeful account of radio station 3UZ's Sunday-morning "Newsbeat" bulletin, which thrusts a microphone in front of car-crash victims and brawl survivors moments after the police and ambulance arrive, delivering Melbourne its weekly dose of actionable gossip that the once-lurid Truth newspaper no longer supplies.
- [About Cigarettes and Gondolas](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/about-cigarettes-and-gondolas/) — Surveys Melbourne's booming cigarette trade and Nobel laureate Macfarlane Burnet's lonely campaign against smoking, then reports the mishap befalling Moomba's imported 16th-century Venetian gondola, which shrank so badly out of water that it now refuses to float.
- [All the Queen's Men](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/all-the-queens-men/) — On the exhausted vocabulary of Royal Tour reporting nine years after "obviously" and "radiant" were banned in 1954, and on Melbourne's noticeably cooler, less crowd-mobbed reception for the Queen's 1963 visit compared with her first.
- [In the Depths of SE 2](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/in-the-depths-of-se-2/) — Follows up on used-car dealer Emmanuel Margolin's spectacular financial collapse with a report from the auction of his Toorak household effects, from leopard-skin rugs and a matador suit tailored in Madrid to the Ford Thunderbird he had already bought twice over.
- [Bunnies in Black Silk Stockings](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/bunnies-in-black-silk-stockings/) — A dispatch from Melbourne's new Playboy Restaurant, the local answer to Hugh Hefner's American bunny clubs, where five waitresses in bunny tails and 18-inch stockings serve drinks only, chosen from a hundred applicants and forbidden from dating the customers.
- [Those Lucky OYO Men](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/those-lucky-oyo-men/) — A tour of Domain Park, Robin Boyd's new 20-storey "own-your-own-flat" tower opposite the Botanic Gardens, from its Georges furniture and £37,500 penthouses to the view over Government House, the MCG and St Patrick's from its balcony.
- [Getting Publicity for Peanuts](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/getting-publicity-for-peanuts/) — Wangaratta throws everything at the Australian Wool Bureau's national publicity contest, from a 500-guest "Wild Colonial" banquet with Sir Robert Menzies as guest speaker to a week-long bullock-wagon re-enactment of Major Mitchell's 1836 expedition down the Hume Highway.
- [Goodbye to the Glaci](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/goodbye-to-the-glaci/) — Farewells Melbourne's Glaciarium after fire destroyed the pioneering ice rink, recalling its genteel opening in 1906, orchestras, speed skaters and eventual defeat by St Moritz and changing fashions.
- [Where They Scrambled for Ned Kelly's Bones](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/where-they-scrambled-for-ned-kellys-bones/) — Tours the condemned cells and gallows yard of the old Melbourne Gaol, recalling the 1929 demolition works that turned up bones from Ned Kelly's unmarked grave and the scramble of souvenir hunters that followed, before dropping in on a talkative old lag at the City Watchhouse next door.
- [Rosettes in Cream and Gold](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/rosettes-in-cream-and-gold/) — A tour of Victoria's ornate Legislative Council chamber and a survey of its obstructive power over Henry Bolte's government, from a killed Liquor Reform Bill to the enduring mystery of the Legislative Assembly's mace, stolen in 1891 and never recovered.
- [Chloe in the Cultural Centre?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/chloe-in-the-cultural-centre/) — Surveys Melbourne's early-1960s building boom around the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets, from the Flinders Street Station redevelopment to a new cultural centre, and worries aloud that the one thing left untouched, the century-old Young and Jackson's pub and its nude painting of Chloe, might finally be swallowed up.
- [From Prickly Pear to Petroleum](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/from-prickly-pear-to-petroleum/) — A visit to the Queensland oil boomtowns of Tara and Moonie, tracing the district's turn from a prickly-pear-choked backwater once known as 'The Lost Province' into the birthplace of Australia's oil industry, and meeting the selection farmers whose land the oil was found under.
- [Beastliness — Dyed in the Wool](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/beastliness-dyed-in-the-wool/) — Covers the Wool Board's annual fashion showcase at Her Majesty's Theatre, where 1964's advertised colour palette, deliberately 'sulky', 'moody' and 'beastly', is played for laughs against the previous year's wholesome wild-colonial theme.
- [Carping Critics](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/carping-critics/) — Tells how a Fisheries and Wildlife inspector's dawn killing of Ararat's beloved pet carp, Napoleon, provoked a town council uproar and a rueful comment from Premier Bolte, then tracks a beer price rise back to a run on forgotten halfpennies at Melbourne pubs.
- [Vengeance on a Black Mud Altar](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/vengeance-on-a-black-mud-altar/) — Recounts the fevered build-up and mud-soaked revenge match after South Australia handed Victoria its first Melbourne Cricket Ground interstate football loss in 37 years, centred on John Peck's on-field haymaker at Adelaide Oval and the lenient VFL tribunal verdict that followed.
- [Clara Bow, Ronald Colman and All That](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/clara-bow-ronald-colman-and-all-that/) — Marks Hoyts' golden jubilee against the demolition of Melbourne's old Savoy Theatre, tracing the cinema chain's rise from a Bourke Street dentist's magic-lantern hobby to the picture-palace rivalry between the Hoyts Regent and its rival, the State, and the wave of name changes that followed as the old chains contracted under television.
- [When Hoyts was Hoyts](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/when-hoyts-was-hoyts/) — Marks Hoyts' 50th anniversary, from dentist-turned-showman Arthur Russell's 1913 start to the neck-and-neck 1929 opening race between the Regent and the State, alongside the wreckers' demolition of the old Savoy (once the temperance-movement Temperance Hall).
- [Two Million Babies](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/two-million-babies/) — Follows the Melbourne City Council's ballot to crown the city's two-millionth citizen, Sir Rohan Delacombe drawing baby Loretta Johnston's name from a barrel of 1300 contenders, alongside Lord Mayor Maurice Nathan's ceremonial axe-swing on St Kilda Road's aging silver poplars and a survey of migrants arriving on both sides of Britain's colour line.
- [Slacks . . . Well, Yes; Bermudas — No!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/slacks-well-yes-bermudas-no/) — Covers the culture clash when the women's Commonwealth golf tournament brought slacks-wearing Canadian and English players to the strictly skirts-only Royal Melbourne Golf Club, and profiles the vast all-female volunteer army, from starters to personal caddies, that ran the tournament.
- [A Minor Battle in the Snow](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-minor-battle-in-the-snow/) — Traces the escalating advertising war between Volkswagen and BMC over whose small car could rightfully claim to have conquered the Antarctic, a dispute complicated by a Melbourne Herald Book Club biography of Sir Hubert Wilkins and the discovery that Shackleton had beaten them both to it in 1906, before closing on a lavish Hickok cuff-link launch that inexplicably got no press coverage at all.
- [Salvation in the Sheep Pavilion](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/salvation-in-the-sheep-pavilion/) — Reports from the Jehovah's Witnesses' 'Everlasting Good News Assembly' at the Melbourne Showground, where over 12,000 delegates packed the sheep pavilion to hear Brooklyn vice-president F. W. Franz preach Armageddon, and profiles door-knocking organiser Donald Maclean on the sect's rapid Australian growth.
- [A Demand for Breathless Enthusiasm: 2. Corinne Kerby — Sole Survivor Among Women Comperes](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-demand-for-breathless-enthusiasm-2-corinne-kerby/) — Profiles Corinne Kerby, the ABC's 'First Lady of television' and the only woman compere to survive from Australian TV's earliest days, tracing her accidental start reading news at the ABC, her live on-air nerves beside newsreader John Royle, her antique-crammed Brighton house, and her ambition to live on a Greek island for a year.
- [Evolution of a Civic Egg](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/evolution-of-a-civic-egg/) — Explains how Melbourne's Lord Mayoralty is quietly decided each year by the Civic Group's backroom seniority system rather than any real election, tracing Leo Curtis's uncontested rise to the chain of office, before turning to Fitzroy's new Lady Mayor and the narrow defeat of junkyard millionairess 'Ma' Dalley in Kew.
- [A Ruined Week (No Paranoia)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/a-ruined-week-no-paranoia/) — Surveys a week of civic drama, a State Electricity Commission strike that blacked out television for two nights running, the tabled King's Bridge royal commission report, and the VFL tribunal hearing that suspended Ron Barassi and John Peck on the eve of the finals.
- [Ships That Knock the Rock](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/ships-that-knock-the-rock/) — Follows the political stoush over Corsair Rock, the submerged hazard at Port Phillip Heads that holed two coastal freighters within a week, pitting Henry Bolte's government against an opposition demanding it be blasted away, and closes on a wistful case for reviving the old Port Phillip Bay paddle steamers.
- [Eaters — and Revolving Drinkers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/eaters-and-revolving-drinkers/) — Tours Melbourne's calorie-conscious boom, from Albert Park's new circular-bar restaurant and Collins Street's steak house Capers, through to health guru Lelord Kordel's free Myer lectures pitched, rather transparently, at selling his own diet books.
- [Aussie Rules — In and Out of Season](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/aussie-rules-in-and-out-of-season/) — Recounts Geelong's first VFL premiership in 11 years, the frantic logistics that got federal minister Hubert Opperman to the Grand Final on time, and the mock-solemn burial of a sparrowhawk (standing in for the vanquished Hawthorn) staged the next day at Kardinia Park by ruckman John Watts, plus MCC secretary Ian Johnson's plans to lift the MCG to a 150,000 capacity.
- [Red Robes and Hot Whiskers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/red-robes-and-hot-whiskers/) — Goes behind the scenes at Myer's Santa Claus School, a 28-subject course modelled on America's original Santa Claus Inc. that trains a whole football team's worth of department-store Fathers Christmas each November, complete with reindeer consultants, hidden microphones and a graduation degree in Bachelor of Santa Claus.
- [The Cup — 1890, Now That Really Was a Cup Year!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-cup-1890-now-that-really-was-a-cup-year/) — A Melbourne Cup Day feature tracing the race from R. C. Bagot's founding of the VRC and Carbine's legendary 1890 win through to the modern Spring Carnival, covering declining Flemington attendances, TAB turnover, the Sandown Park merger fight, and the 1861 saga of the first Cup winner, Archer, walked over 550 miles from Nowra to Melbourne.
- [What About the Arts — and the Kittens?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/what-about-the-arts-and-the-kittens/) — Defends Melbourne's civic pride against a Sydney magazine's charge of drab mediocrity, then traces the theft of a display-only Melbourne Gold Cup replica lent to New Zealand's Tourist Bureau, a farce compounded when the genuine trophy had to travel there in its place for a building opening days later.
- [The Girls in the Golden Frames](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-girls-in-the-golden-frames/) — Traces Melbourne's pub counter-lunch tradition from its Edwardian heyday through its 1949 revival, then profiles the Hotel Britannia's latest innovation, cigarette girls turned 'living pictures', posed motionless for hours in a gilt frame above the bar to boost trade.
- [The Electronic Sir Robert](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-electronic-sir-robert/) — Compares the television staging of Robert Menzies' and Arthur Calwell's 1963 election policy speeches, from Menzies' pre-recorded GTV-9 performance before an invited Kooyong audience to a stray piece of electronic magic that broadcast Calwell's speech straight into a J. C. Williamson's theatre audience mid-performance, and notes a young Bob Hawke launching his own campaign against Hubert Opperman in Corio.
- [Christmas across a continent](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/christmas-across-a-continent/) — A survey of how Australians spend Christmas Day across wildly different settings, from turkey conservatives at Rosebud and water-skiing Santas at Surfers Paradise to Warramunga camps, Antarctic research bases, and mail runs to Cocos Island and Tasman Island lighthouse.
- [More Blood Than Ben Casey](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/more-blood-than-ben-casey/) — Skewers the Mornington Shire Council's banning of Enid Blyton's Noddy from the Peninsula Regional Library Service as hasty and sloppy, then hunts down an unabridged Brothers Grimm collection to show just how much decapitation, cannibalism and gore actually passes for classic children's literature next to Blyton's mild offences.
- [Used Cars and Gorgeous Capes](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/used-cars-and-gorgeous-capes/) — Surveys Melbourne's colourful used-car dealer scene, from Kevin Dennis's face-everywhere self-promotion to the theatrical bidding wars at the north-end car auctions, before tracking the spectacular comeback of Emmanuel Margolin, ruined by the credit squeeze and a Ford Australia falling-out, now rebuilding from Moonee Ponds with a Marie Antoinette gilt suite and a Madrid matador's cape collection to his name.
- [Vale, Osiris and the Mighty Wurlitzer!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/vale-osiris-and-the-mighty-wurlitzer/) — Marks the closure of Walter Burley Griffin's Capitol Theatre on Swanston Street, the first dinkum de-luxe movie palace in the Southern Hemisphere since its 1924 opening with 'The Ten Commandments', and surveys the broader decline of Melbourne's grand old picture palaces as the State splits into the Forum and the Rapallo.
- [Rivelazioni Sui Delitti . . .](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/rivelazioni-sui-delitti/) — Profiles Il Globo, the Italian-language newspaper whose fearless reporting exposed extortion rackets at Melbourne's Victoria Market, and surveys the wave of market-related shootings and huge, Continental-style funerals that followed the death of reputed 'Honoured Society' boss Domenico Italiano, 'Il Papa'.
- [Like 80 Holdens Doing 80 MPH](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/like-80-holdens-doing-80-mph/) — Reports from Avalon on the handover of the first Australian-built Mirage III jet fighter, tracing the French-negotiated contract from Sir Lawrence Wackett and Sir Richard Williams's early aviation pioneering days through to the new fighter's 90-gallon-a-minute fuel thirst and its taciturn, French-trained RAAF test pilots.
- [Whatever Became of Those Sane Drinkers?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/whatever-became-of-those-sane-drinkers/) — Surveys Victoria's long, thwarted history of liquor licensing reform, from wartime six o'clock closing through failed Bolte government bills and a Judge Fraser world pub-crawl commissioned to study the question, to the new Royal Commission under P. D. Phillips, QC, and its startling revelation of an eight-year-old girl introduced to wine by her own father.
- [Pies — Black, Brindle, and Golden](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/pies-black-brindle-and-golden/) — Profiles Les McClure, the self-described 'little b----r from the country' who built Four'n Twenty into a 59-van pie empire before selling out to Peters, then rebuilt a second pie and catering fortune from Bendigo and St Kilda Road, gimmick telephones, pop-up toasters and all.
- [When Flappers Fluttered Through the Flames](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/when-flappers-fluttered-through-the-flames/) — Marks Melbourne's belated 1964 premiere of 'Cleopatra' at the renamed Cleopatra Theatre, then traces the cinema's own history back through the Lyceum and Paramount names to its 1915 opening with Mary Pickford in 'Rags', and the sensational 1916 season of Theda Bara in 'Carmen'.
- [Try These If You Can't Buy "The Group"](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/try-these-if-you-cant-buy-the-group/) — A satirical survey of the pulp novels, nudist magazines and lurid historical potboilers Melburnians were reduced to buying after the banning of Mary McCarthy's 'The Group', from naturist club newsletters to a florid account of the real Sir Francis Dashwood's Hell Fire Club.
- [From an Unknown Saint to Mother's Milk](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/from-an-unknown-saint-to-mothers-milk/) — Unpacks the furore over St Kilda Football Club's proposed 1965 move from the St Kilda Cricket Ground to booming, aboriginally-named Moorabbin, weighing club finances and a possible VFA merger against the wider anxiety that football, soccer and cricket are all now scrambling over the same shrinking supply of suburban grounds.
- [When Melbourne Has 4.6 Million People . . .](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/when-melbourne-has-4.6-million-people/) — Gleefully projects Melbourne's population overtaking Sydney's by 1985 using National Cash Register's computer forecasts, then tours the just-finished National Mutual Centre, briefly Australia's biggest building, as the latest shot in a decades-long Melbourne-Sydney skyscraper rivalry that began with the ICI Building and the Conzinc Riotinto tower.
- [The Explosive Vino di Carlton and Fitzroy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-04-25-the-explosive-vino-di-carlton-and-fitzroy/) — A survey of Melbourne's home wine-making boom, centred on Carlton and Fitzroy, where tens of thousands of Italian and Greek families were producing a million gallons a year in backyard stills and laundry sinks.
- [Melbourne's Evergreen Exhibition](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/melbournes-evergreen-exhibition/) — A history of Melbourne's Exhibition Building, from the lavish international exhibitions of 1880 and 1888 through Sidney Myer's Depression-era Christmas dinner for 11,000 unemployed people to its 1963 revival as a trade fair venue.
- [The Monash Story: Keeping Them Down on the Farm](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-05-02-the-monash-story-7-keeping-them-down-on-the-farm-melbourne-s-other-university/) — A portrait of Monash University three years after its unexpectedly early opening, examining its car-dependent Clayton campus, its race to become the world's fastest-growing university, its chronic underfunding, and the outsized personalities shaping its character.
- [Black Sunday for the Port Girls](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-05-09-black-sunday-for-the-port-girls/) — The arrival of a Soviet whaling fleet of 34 ships in Melbourne, including the world's largest whaling vessel the Sovietskaya Ukraina, and the failed attempts by Melburnians to fraternise with the crew on a shut Sunday.
- [The Oyohus of the Pram Belt](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-05-16-the-oyohus-of-the-pram-belt/) — A tour of the outer-suburban display-home craze gripping Melbourne in 1964, from the traffic-snarled exposition villages of East Doncaster to the Brotherhood of St Laurence's grim report on 55,000 families unable to afford decent housing.
- [Mersey Millionaires v. the Kelly Gang](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-05-23-mersey-millionaires-v-the-kelly-gang/) — Everton Football Club's 1964 tour of Melbourne, in which the English champions thrashed a controversially New South Wales-loaded Australian soccer side 8-2 at Olympic Park before a record crowd of 32,450, with the visitors so superior their right-half scored three goals after being switched to forward.
- [Science with Sherry, Moselle and Cognac](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-05-30-science-with-sherry-moselle-and-cognac/) — Royal Commissioner P. D. Phillips stages a scientifically monitored dinner party at Melbourne University's University House, complete with breathalyser readings, to test what really happens to guests who drink moderately at a convivial dinner.
- [Science — With Sherry, Moselle and Cognac](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/science-with-sherry-moselle-and-cognac/) — Follows Royal Commissioner P. D. Phillips's liquor inquiry into a University House test dinner, where a pathologist, a police surgeon and a breathalyser scientifically tracked exactly how much sherry, wine, port and cognac a table of brewers, clergy and academics could drink over one long, very enjoyable meal.
- [Now Watch Out for Those Inside Stories!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-06-06-now-watch-out-for-those-inside-stories/) — Keith Dunstan enrols at the Australian Academy of Investigation, a Collins Street school for private detectives run by a former Melbourne CIB man, and is disillusioned to find the work is mostly insurance claims and divorce surveillance, not espionage.
- [Eyestrain for Art's Sake](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-06-13-eyestrain-for-arts-sake/) — Keith Dunstan surveys the 13th Melbourne International Film Festival at the Palais Theatre in St Kilda, celebrating its world-class program while lamenting the bureaucratic obstacles of censorship and customs restrictions that hamper what is one of the world's finest film festivals.
- [A Noble £10m Home for a Noble Game](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-06-20-a-noble-10m-home-for-a-noble-game/) — The Victorian Football League unveils plans for a vast new stadium at Waverley, to hold 157,000 spectators and cost £14 million for its first stage, prompting Keith Dunstan to weigh the ambition against the practical difficulties of financing it and luring crowds 15 miles from the city.
- [Mud Crabs for Boys, Scallops for All](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-06-27-mud-crabs-for-boys-scallops-for-all/) — Melbourne has become the headquarters of a booming scallop industry, with 90 boats working Port Phillip Bay and five million scallops a month being dredged, a transformation Keith Dunstan celebrates as one of the best things to happen to the city since Baron von Mueller designed the Botanic Gardens.
- [A Feasibility Study of a Hot Potato](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-07-04-a-feasibility-study-of-a-hot-potato/) — Melbourne's push to host a World Fair in the early 1970s, led by Lord Mayor Leo Curtis and former Lord Mayor Sir Maurice Nathan, who lobbied Prime Minister Sir Robert Menzies and sought £50,000 from local backers to fund a feasibility study, with Essendon Airport floated as the ideal site once civil aviation vacated it for Tullamarine.
- [O, the Opulence of O!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-07-11-o-the-opulence-of-o/) — A behind-the-scenes tour of Reg Ansett's Austarama TV studio at Nunawading, showcasing the opulent new Channel O before its August 1964 launch, with a pointed reminder of Ansett's 1963 promise to show Australians what Australia has to offer.
- [Life at Jervis Bay: No Longer Turning Australian Boys into Englishmen](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-07-25-life-at-jervis-bay-no-longer-turning-australian-boys-into-englishmen/) — A detailed visit to the Royal Australian Naval College at Jervis Bay on graduation day, tracing the college's turbulent history from its 1910 founding through near-closure in the 1930s, and examining how it recovered from the HMAS Voyager disaster while modernising its English-school traditions.
- [Penguins, Pies, and Megapodes](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-08-01-penguins-pies-and-megapodes/) — The Mallee Fowl, a remarkable megapode bird facing extinction, gets a new 15,000-acre wildlife reserve near Mildura following advocacy by the Victorian Fisheries and Wildlife Department, with the Penguin Parade at Phillip Island and lyrebirds at Sherbrooke Forest rounding out Victoria's bird attractions for the growing flood of American birdwatching tourists.
- [Dialling for a Prayer and a Bet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-08-08-dialling-for-a-prayer-and-a-bet/) — Victoria's Totalisator Agency Board has quietly become a £40-million-a-year institution, bringing off-course betting into sterile shopfronts next to pubs and banks while channelling millions to hospitals, charities and racing clubs, as New South Wales and South Australia move to adopt the same system.
- [No Sunday Tumbling or Burletta Yet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-08-15-no-sunday-tumbling-or-burletta-yet/) — A survey of Melbourne's Sunday laws, tracing the Sabbatarian battles of the 1880s through to Chief Secretary Arthur Rylah's cautious 1964 suggestion that theatres might open on Sundays, and the near-total public silence that greeted it.
- [Queuing for the Final Cachet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-08-22-queuing-for-the-final-cachet/) — A portrait of Melbourne's devotion to queuing for VFL finals tickets, following two Essendon supporters who camped outside the MCG for days through snow and wind and ultimately charmed the Melbourne Cricket Club secretary over toast cooked on a primus stove.
- [Night of High Drama](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-09-05-night-of-high-drama/) — The annual race between Melbourne television stations GTV-9 and HSV-7 to be first on air with the Brownlow Medal winner, a battle won five years running by HSV's Mike Williamson through a combination of pre-taped interviews, hidden surveillance and a terrifying drive through Elsternwick Junction.
- [The Rag Trade: 'A Goddamn Crazy Business...'](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-09-05-the-rag-trade-a-goddamn-crazy-business/) — A four-page portrait of Melbourne's garment industry centred on Flinders Lane, tracing its history from the great warehouses of the pre-war era through the rise of specialist manufacturers, the menace of design pirates, the problem of bad debts, and the perpetual uncertainty of guessing what women will wear two years hence.
- [The Week of the Great White Fleet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-09-12-the-week-of-the-great-white-fleet/) — A comparison of the 1964 American warship visit to Melbourne with the legendary 1908 arrival of the Great White Fleet, when 16 battleships under Admiral Sperry drew half a million people to the city in a single day and the party for naval ratings at the Exhibition Building outshone every other entertainment of the tour.
- [For Tourists: Pies, Hares, and Cast-Iron](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-09-19-for-tourists-pies-hares-and-cast-iron/) — A satirical tourism plan for Melbourne, proposing pie-factory visits, live hare coursing, Percy Cerutty runs up the Portsea sandhills, and the restoration of Little Lonsdale Street's seedy glamour to pull American visitors away from the sinful East.
- [Bacterial Life in a Stiff Collar: Those Were the Days at Geelong](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-09-26-bacterial-life-in-a-stiff-collar-those-were-the-days-at-geelong/) — Keith Dunstan recalls his years boarding at Geelong Grammar School, from the cold showers, fagging duties and Saturday-morning bullying to the towering authority of headmaster James Ralph Darling and the Left-wing staff who challenged the boys to think for themselves.
- [High Jinks in the Hard Top](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-10-03-high-jinks-in-the-hard-top/) — A tour of Melbourne's ambitious new entertainment projects, including the Palladium Entertainment Centre with its twin theatres and Maxim's restaurant, and a rival rooftop licensed restaurant opening on Melbourne Cup eve at the National Mutual Centre.
- [Mr Borg's Auction in SE2](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-10-10-mr-borgs-auction-in-se2/) — A vivid account of the Toorak household auction of Raymond Borg's house in Yarradale Road, where the crowd's main fascination was watching used-car dealer Emmanuel Margolin quietly buy back the Ming bronzes, Sevres vases and stuffed eagle he had been forced to sell at an earlier auction during the credit squeeze.
- [What's Been Missin' from Kissin'](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-10-17-whats-been-missin-from-kissin/) — A report on the Cutex flavoured-lipstick launch party in Melbourne, where Cherry Kiss, Peppermint Kiss and Caramel Kiss were unveiled to an audience including Footscray captain-coach Ted Whitten, with the assembled press left to judge whether taste and fragrance really did add a new dimension to cosmetics.
- [A Century Could Be Just Around the Bend](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-10-24-a-century-could-be-just-around-the-bend/) — A sharp critique of the Victorian Railways' chronic derailment problem and its causes, tracing the system's 'muddled economy' back to a 1949 British transport expert's report that found the VR strangled by political interference, fantastically cheap freight rates, and a shortage of staff that any private employer could have solved by paying above award.
- [There's a Whispering War Up There](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-10-31-theres-a-whispering-war-up-there/) — A ringside account of the publicity battle between TAA and Ansett-ANA over the arrival of Melbourne's first Boeing 727 jets, from competing proving flights to beer-bottle balancing at 31,000 feet.
- [The Moss Spreads in Spring Street](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-11-07-the-moss-spreads-in-spring-street/) — A history of Victoria's ferocious Liberal-Country Party rivalry, from the 1921 fall of the Lawson government to the 1964 supply crisis in which Country Party leader Moss forced a complete surrender from Premier Bolte.
- [Point Cook: More Choosy Than Ever](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-11-21-sect-objectors-point-cook-more-choosy-than-ever/) — A profile of the RAAF's officer training academy at Point Cook, tracing the base's history from Sir Richard Williams's first flight in 1914 to the newly degree-granting RAAF Academy of 1964, where cadets study physics alongside their flying.
- [Oh, Bondi! Oh, Surfers! Oh, OH, St. Kilda!](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-11-28-oh-bondi-oh-surfers-oh-oh-st-kilda/) — The campaign by Melbourne's Victorian Federation of Catholic Mothers to ban bikinis from bayside beaches prompts a survey of the unlikely coalition of voices for and against, from Ron Barassi's wife to Premier Bolte and the bikini manufacturer who announced he would double production.
- [Adventures of a Would-be Wine Snob](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/adventures-of-a-would-be-wine-snob/) — A home bottler's tour of Victoria's wine industry in 1964, from siphoning hogsheads into gallon flasks at kitchen tables to a wineabout through Rutherglen's Morris and All Saints vineyards and Nagambie's Chateau Tahbilk.
- [Do You Ken Yon Peal?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-12-05-do-you-ken-yon-peal/) — Inside the locked bell tower of St Paul's Cathedral, Melbourne, as an interstate team of ten ringers attempts the longest full peal ever recorded there, three hours and forty-eight minutes of non-stop mathematical ringing on the only 12-bell set outside the British Isles.
- [The Hot Dog is Still Too Thin / Radio Australia: The World's Most Successful](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-12-19-the-hot-dog-is-still-too-thin-radio-australia-the-world-s-most-/) — On the eve of Radio Australia's 25th birthday, a visit to its cramped Melbourne headquarters reveals the world's most-listened-to overseas radio service, ahead of the BBC and Voice of America, sustained by a quarter-million letters a year from listeners across Asia.
- [You Need More Than a 'D' in Toorak](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1964-12-26-you-need-more-than-a-d-in-toorak/) — The opening of 'Nareeb', Toorak's last great private estate, for public auction draws 15,000 visitors to the 53-acre Kooyong Road property unchanged since 1888, where the contents, from a 1920 Rolls-Royce to aspidistras, sell for over £18,000.
- [The "Perfidy" of Ron Barassi](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-01-09-the-perfidy-of-ron-barassi/) — Melbourne Football Club's greatest player and vice-captain, Ron Barassi, stuns the city by accepting the playing-coach role at rival Carlton, raising questions about loyalties, pet budgies taught to cheer for the Demons, and the court case that cost Melbourne the 1963 premiership.
- [The Girl Who Came Back](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-01-16-the-girl-who-came-back/) — An interview with Diane McNiece, the Melbourne woman who answered a newspaper plea from the 150 lonely men of Tennant Creek and returned a local celebrity, with swollen legs, 40 proposals and a fund of stories from the Northern Territory.
- [There's Money in Ned Kelly](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-01-23-theres-money-in-ned-kelly/) — The Australian National Travel Association's reluctance to exploit the Ned Kelly legend as a tourist attraction, while the Institute of Applied Science banishes his armour to the basement and the Government plans to demolish Melbourne Gaol where Kelly was hanged.
- [What Sort of School?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-02-06-what-sort-of-school/) — A two-part examination of the class anxieties and practical calculations behind Melbourne parents' choices between state and private schools, with Batman weighing snobbery, church, facilities and self-confidence, and philosopher Max Charlesworth arguing from John Stuart Mill for the Catholic right to choose.
- [The Ultimate Status Symbol](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-02-20-the-ultimate-status-symbol/) — A tour of the 31st Melbourne Motor Show at the Exhibition Building, where the millionth Holden shared floor space with a £17,000 Mercedes 600 built for heads of state, a Rolls-Royce Silver Cloud III and a hand-made Ferrari, all in a city with no completed freeway to drive them on.
- [Gin and Chicken on HD Day](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-02-27-gin-and-chicken-on-hd-day/) — The elaborate theatre of GM-H's "inverse public relations" strategy for the new Holden HD launch, whereby keeping the car out of the motor show for four days generated far more front-page coverage than a conventional opening-day unveiling would have done.
- [The Day of the Herefords](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-03-06-the-day-of-the-herefords/) — The South Boorook annual Hereford stud cattle sale near Mortlake, where Western District graziers arrive by Cessna and Rolls-Royce to bid in guineas for the last time before decimal currency, with piped music, machine-gun auctioneers and ten kegs of beer at the end.
- [A Touch of Gogol](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-03-13-a-touch-of-gogol/) — Showman Eric Edgley's three-year ordeal to bring the Moscow State Circus to Melbourne for Moomba, including battles with animal welfare groups over the tigers, quarantine tangles that seemed to implicate Sir Robert Menzies in a Kremlin plot, and the awkward post-show drinks party where the Russians stood at one end and the Australians at the other.
- [All the Fun of the Ferry](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-03-20-all-the-fun-of-the-ferry/) — A report on Melbourne's Moomba festival, tracing how it grew from the old Eight-hour Day trade union procession into a city-wide holiday spectacle, with Sydney's Manly ferry North Head the unexpected hit of the week on the Yarra.
- [Just an Anonymous Airport](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-03-27-just-an-anonymous-airport/) — The Federal Government's failure to fund terminal buildings at Melbourne's new Tullamarine airport reignites the Melbourne-Sydney rivalry, with Melbourne's Tullamarine boosters warning the city risks disappearing from international air maps entirely.
- [Anyone Here from Ballarat?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-04-03-anyone-here-from-ballarat/) — A tour of Ballarat, the Victorian goldfields city that once held itself to be the grandest inland city in the British Empire, examining its extraordinary statues, threatened iron-lace verandahs, decaying gold-rush hotels, and modest hopes for a future as a tourist and cultural centre.
- [Dogs Chasing Each Other's Tails](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-04-10-dogs-chasing-each-others-tails/) — The 14th Australian Architectural Convention debates the chaotic state of Melbourne's planning, with Harry Seidler lamenting the two-to-one height formula and architects mourning the imminent demolition of Walter Burley Griffin's Capitol Theatre for a shopping arcade.
- [Having Trouble in Low Joints](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-04-17-having-trouble-in-low-joints/) — The devastating Victorian drought has turned football grounds to concrete, producing a season of cartilage injuries so frequent and so meticulously reported that any reader can follow the medical literature without a medical degree.
- [Dawn of a New Golden Age](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-04-24-dawn-of-a-new-golden-age/) — A behind-the-scenes account of the lavish promotional campaign Hoyts mounted for the Melbourne premiere of Goldfinger, from painted-gold television models and purloined Bond-girl display panels to kits containing white roses and toy revolvers.
- [There's Money in Mulga](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-05-01-theres-money-in-mulga/) — A tour through Australia's souvenir trade with John Frost, Melbourne's leading souvenir man, reveals a booming export business in mulga woodwork, metalised kangaroo skins and five-foot stuffed koalas destined for Asian department stores and the occasional eccentric American film producer.
- [Battle of the Flower](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/battle-of-the-flower/) — A tour of Australia's competitive gardening culture and its flower festivals, from Toowoomba's Carnival of Flowers and Ballarat's begonias to the Sydney Morning Herald's statewide garden contest and Western Australia's wildflower season.
- [London in Melbourne](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-05-15-london-in-melbourne/) — Two encounters at Melbourne's Tivoli and Menzies Hotel, one with English comedian Max Bygraves preparing nervously for his opening night and one with American singer Julie London defending her habit of stripping to a leotard for an audience of Melbourne critics who found it alarming.
- [Bolte Plays Ring-a-rosy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-05-22-bolte-plays-ring-a-rosy/) — Melbourne's almost total absence of freeways, while Sydney and American cities forge ahead, traced to the Victorian Country Party's stranglehold on the Legislative Council and its repeated blocking of Henry Bolte's road-funding proposals.
- [A Mural for 1000 Years](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-05-29-a-mural-for-1000-years/) — A profile of Melbourne artist Stanislaus Ostoja-Kotkowski, who fuses electronics, laser science and industrial pigments into mural works for BP buildings in Melbourne and Adelaide, and who trained at the National Gallery under William Dargie while cutting sandwiches through the night to stay fed.
- [The View from the High Rise](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-06-05-the-view-from-the-high-rise/) — The Victorian Housing Commission's ambitious high-rise estates, rising in concrete at Carlton, Fitzroy, North Melbourne and Flemington, are remaking the inner suburbs faster than the VFL has noticed, packing 1470 people into estates where 439 once lived, while families navigate the novel pleasures and hardships of the pigeon loft.
- [A Town Like Churchill](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-06-12-a-town-like-churchill/) — The brand new Latrobe Valley satellite town named after Winston Churchill faces a determined citizens' campaign to rename it Hazelwood, led by dairy farmer Tom Lawless, who erects signs, circulates petitions and ambushes visiting parliamentarians with billboards at the station.
- [The Punter and the Crematorium](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-06-19-the-punter-and-the-crematorium/) — A tour of the brand-new Sandown Racecourse on its first season, examining its extraordinary television-equipped grandstand, the complicated finances shared between the VATC, the VRC and the Moonee Valley Racing Club, and the cheerful fact that the track sits directly opposite the Springvale Crematorium.
- [No Biz Like Snow Biz](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-06-26-no-biz-like-snow-biz/) — The opening of the 1965 ski season at Mount Buller, where a new heated outdoor pool, the Bull's Blood Bar, and a string of glittering lodge parties mark Victoria's booming snowfields, though the state's fragmented government control of its mountains leaves them lagging far behind the privately run NSW snowfields.
- [The Agony of King Kong](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-07-03-the-agony-of-king-kong/) — ATV-0's attempt to revive the 1933 classic 'King Kong' on Monday-night television was blocked by the Commonwealth Film Censor, touching off a debate about censorship, nostalgia and the ape's ill-fated passion for Fay Wray.
- [Sunday After Evensong](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-07-10-sunday-after-evensong/) — Victoria's ban on Sunday cinema screenings is challenged by moves from New South Wales, and Melbourne theatre managers and clergymen stake out their positions on whether picture houses should open after evening church.
- [Pushing Through Solid Mink](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-07-17-pushing-through-solid-mink/) — Joan Sutherland's triumphant return to Melbourne for the Sutherland-Williamson-International Grand Opera Company's opening night draws comparisons with Dame Nellie Melba's equally sensational homecoming in 1902.
- [The Bonynge Affair](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-07-24-the-bonynge-affair/) — The Sutherland-Williamson-International Grand Opera Company's Melbourne season is overshadowed by the acrimonious departure of conductor John Matheson after clashes with Richard Bonynge, leaving J. C. Williamson's scrambling to fill the non-Sutherland nights.
- [Like When King Edward Abdicated](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/like-when-king-edward-abdicated/) — Norm Smith's sacking and sudden reinstatement as Melbourne's football coach send the city into mourning, saturate the newspapers and television, and expose the club's patrician habits.
- [Just Waiting for Chaos Day](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-08-14-just-waiting-for-chaos-day/) — Chartered accountant R. W. Parry has spent two years campaigning against Australia's decimal currency changeover, predicting the country will run out of coins within days of the February 1966 introduction and that vending machines will jam throughout the country.
- [The Needling of Needle Ned](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-08-21-the-needling-of-needle-ned/) — Melbourne rheumatologist Dr Michael Kelly, nicknamed 'Needle Ned' by wartime soldiers, has waged a one-man campaign against what he considers the medical profession's myths about high blood pressure, anti-coagulants, cortisone, the Pill and cancer radiotherapy.
- [Mr Fudge Knows His S.E.2](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-09-11-mr-fudge-knows-his-se2/) — Melbourne developer H. J. Fudge's plan to subdivide Nareeb, the last of Toorak's great mansions, into 20 luxury house lots at up to £39,000 each marks a turning point in the postcode rivalry between Toorak S.E.2 and the newly chic South Yarra S.E.1.
- [Lady Chatterley Comes to Town](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-09-18-lady-chatterley-comes-to-town/) — After a lifetime as a protected Victorian, Keith Dunstan reads D. H. Lawrence's 'Lady Chatterley's Lover' and reports back on its remarkable preoccupation with buttocks, its game-keeper hero's unlikely gentlemanly credentials, and its curiously unfinished ending.
- [Norm and I Adore Satire and Yoga](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-09-25-norm-and-i-adore-satire-and-yoga/) — Barry Humphries returns to Melbourne from London, more polished and confident, with a new show at the Comedy Theatre, an updated Mrs Norm Everage who now does yoga and hangs her own pasta on the clothesline, and stories of waiting outside the Savoy in drag to ambush the Prime Minister.
- [Pop Goes the Cash Register](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-10-02-pop-goes-the-cash-register/) — The Australian pop music scene in 1965, when local acts began outselling imported British and American records on Melbourne radio charts, with music industry figure Ron Tudor charting how groups like the Easybeats, Billy Thorpe and the Aztecs, and the Seekers had finally found a way to compete.
- [Captain Lancey Forges Ahead](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-10-09-captain-lancey-forges-ahead/) — A review of Agnes Paton Bell's new history 'Melbourne: John Batman's Village', which while beautifully produced is frustratingly vague about whether it was Batman, Fawkner, or Captain Lancey who actually founded the city, and skips lightly over the financial panics and social upheavals that made Melbourne what it became.
- [Marlene Dietrich and the Press Gang](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-10-16-marlene-dietrich-and-the-press-gang/) — Dietrich holds a single tightly managed press conference at the Southern Cross Hotel, revealing her opinions on Germany, Paris, Frank Sinatra and the Beatles, while deflecting every question about her legs, her family and whether her sex appeal was ever real.
- [You Can't Get Much Lusher](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-10-23-you-cant-get-much-lusher/) — The Fabulous Lido, a lavish theatre-restaurant in Melbourne's old Savoy building, is about to open, with millionaire ex-dancer David Hamilton McIlwraith pouring half a million pounds into gold mosaic tiles, chandeliers imported from Egypt and long-legged hand-picked showgirls.
- [Melbourne's Sacred Rites](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-10-30-melbournes-sacred-rites-cup-day-is-not-for-racing/) — A survey of the Melbourne Cup carnival's elaborate rituals, from the Governor-General's mounted procession down the straight to the champagne-and-chicken-sandwich car park rites, arguing that serious racegoers prefer Derby Day and that the Cup itself is just a gloriously open handicap.
- [Timbertop and the Disposal Store](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-11-06-timbertop-and-the-disposal-store/) — The arrival of Prince Charles at Geelong Grammar's bush campus Timbertop sends Melbourne into a frenzy of rumour, snobbishness and sightseeing, while a nearby Malvern house that once belonged to a former owner becomes an unlikely tourist attraction drawing streams of cars on weekends.
- [How Afferbeck Lauder's Life Was Changed](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-11-20-how-afferbeck-lauders-life-was-changed/) — Alistair Morrison, the Sydney design consultant behind the Strine phenomenon, reveals how a chance incident at a bookshop involving Monica Dickens triggered 'Let Stalk Strine', how he concealed his identity for months, and how sudden national fame under an assumed name left him feeling like a con man.
- [Batman Crosses the Murray](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-11-27-batman-crosses-the-murray/) — A visit to Sydney forces a grudging admission that the city is gaining an edge on Melbourne, with superior old and new buildings, easier taxi access, cheaper public transport and a Sydney Opera House that, from a distance at least, looks glorious.
- [One and a Half Million Bottles of Champagne](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-12-04-one-and-a-half-million-bottles-of-champagne/) — Victoria's historic wineries at Great Western and All Saints, Wahgunyah, receive National Trust plaques in the same week, prompting a tour of Great Western's 34 miles of underground drives and a visit to the castellated All Saints winery, whose Sutherland Smith family have kept Rutherglen's wine tradition alive since the 1860s despite phylloxera wiping out much of the region.
- [No Openings for Henry Bolte](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-12-11-no-openings-for-henry-bolte/) — The insurance building boom transforms Melbourne's William Street, with Sir Robert Menzies cornering the market on grand openings while the old St James building makes way for a new AMP tower designed by American architects Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.
- [The Last Swill](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-12-18-the-last-swill/) — Victoria's 49-year-old six o'clock closing finally ends, ushering in 10 p.m. trading and a rush of late-night pub entertainment, restaurants with beer licences, and a new .05 blood-alcohol limit for drivers.
- [Cannery Row at the Test](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1965-12-25-cannery-row-at-the-test/) — A report on the rain-ruined First Test at the Woolloongabba in Brisbane, where Doug Walters made a brilliant debut century despite Fred Titmus and monsoon weather, Bill Lawry scored a dogged 166 amid a bitter disputed catch controversy, and the barracking from under the Moreton Bay figs rivalled the cricket for entertainment.
- [Taking Your Pick at Rosebud](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-01-08-taking-your-pick-at-rosebud/) — A tour of the summer camping hierarchy along the Mornington Peninsula, from Rosebud's 5000-person tent city through Rye's middle ground to the discreet Toorak-in-January refinement of Portsea, where land sells for £18,000 a block and even a surfboard rack confers social distinction.
- [The Battle for Prince Charles](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-02-12-the-battle-for-prince-charles/) — A reporter's-eye account of the press corps's elaborate, futile attempts to photograph Prince Charles during his 1966 Australian visit, from rooftop vigils outside Canberra's Government House to car chases through the suburbs of the capital in underpowered Holdens.
- [The Big Strike and Late Closing](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-02-19-the-big-strike-and-late-closing/) — A sardonic dispatch from strike-bound Melbourne in February 1966, where a Victorian public servants' walkout brought empty city bars, warm beer and candlelight, while the pubs that survived thrived under the newly extended 10 o'clock trading hours, and Chloe continued to bare all at Young and Jackson's for another 30 hours a week.
- [Nostalgia — Terribly, Terribly In](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-02-26-nostalgia-terribly-terribly-in/) — A survey of Melbourne's 1966 craze for Victorian and Edwardian restaurant decor, from coach lamps and wrought-iron balustrades to gas-lit pianola rolls and flower pots as ice buckets, in which a new restaurant built from 3000 beer cans collected at the MCG may be the only truly Melburnian establishment of the lot.
- [Keeping up with Carnaby Street](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-03-05-keeping-up-with-carnaby-street/) — British fashion designers Roger Nelson and Jean Muir arrive in Melbourne to present the mod Regency look for men, double-breasted with six buttons and floral shirts, and confirm that Melbourne's Lord Henry's Gear store in Russell Street is right up with the latest in Carnaby Street.
- [Cole's Funny Books — Funnier Than Ever](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-03-12-coles-funny-books-funnier-than-ever/) — A fond revisit to E.W. Cole's Funny Picture Books, still selling 19,000 copies a year after 90 years and entirely unchanged, featuring Cole's Patent Whipping Machine for Flogging Naughty Boys in School, his Electro-Micro Scolding Machine for Naughty Girls, and his spirited offer of £1000 to anyone who could build a flying machine.
- [Not a Muscovy Duck Type](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-03-19-not-a-muscovy-duck-type/) — A close-up portrait of Harold Holt in his first weeks as Prime Minister, contrasting his open, press-friendly style with Menzies' remote Edwardian grandeur, with an assessment of what a swimming pool where the Muscovy ducks used to be might signify about the Lodge's new occupants.
- [A 900,000 Beer-can Mardi Gras](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-03-26-a-900-000-beer-can-mardi-gras/) — Moomba's eleventh year comes into its own as a genuine street festival, with a parade crowd estimated at 900,000 along Swanston Street, an anti-Vietnam demonstration that pelted television host Graham Kennedy with flour, and the customary carpet of empty beer cans along the Yarra banks.
- [Sulks in the Bedroom](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-04-02-sulks-in-the-bedroom/) — Pat Phoenix, who plays Elsie Tanner in Coronation Street, visits Melbourne on a personal appearance tour and reflects on the programme's grip on its audience, from fans threatening her sailor boyfriend to strangers who left memorial wreaths when Mrs Barlow was killed off.
- [The Mighty Wurlitzer Rose in a Pool of Light.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-mighty-wurlitzer-rose-in-a-pool-of-light/) — A visit to the Regent Theatre's Mighty Wurlitzer organ, one of only two left working in Australia, and a morning practice session with virtuoso organist Tony Fenelon.
- [The Phantom Rolls-Royce](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-04-16-the-phantom-rolls-royce/) — The Melbourne City Council orders a Phantom V Rolls-Royce for the Lord Mayor at $23,800, prompting a survey of the Council's peculiar anachronisms, from the Civic Group's gentlemanly rotation of the mayoralty to the ongoing failure to build a civic square or make sensible use of a city block opposite Myer.
- [Who's Been Working on the Railroad?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-04-30-whos-been-working-on-the-railroad/) — Melbourne's underground railway dream traces a 40-year history of reports, promises, shelved starts and lottery schemes, from the 1929 Metropolitan Town Planning Commission report through the Utah Construction Company's flat offer to build in three years, to the Wilbur Smith and Associates study of 1966 that recommends the same underground the city has been talking about since 1925.
- [The Wall Street End of Collins Street](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-05-07-the-wall-street-end-of-collins-street/) — A lament for the retail and architectural decline of Collins Street's eastern end, as banks and insurance houses squeeze out old shops and new high-rise buildings obliterate the old paving stones, lamps, and Victorian facades.
- [The Battle of the Sly Bakers: 90,000 Illegal Loaves](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-05-14-the-battle-of-the-sly-bakers-90000-illegal-loaves/) — Melbourne's long-running underground war over illegal weekend bread baking, where 90,000 families buy fresh loaves from clandestine Sunday bakeries while union officials and the Trades Hall Council condemn the practice as sweated labour in unsanitary conditions.
- [The Dancing Girls of Little Lon](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-05-21-the-dancing-girls-of-little-lon/) — An interview with ballerina Kathleen Gorham at her new dance academy in Little Lonsdale Street, where she reflects on her twenty-year career with the Borovansky Ballet and Australian Ballet, her admiration for Robert Helpmann and Margot Fonteyn, and her decision to retire from performance.
- [Preparing for an Invasion](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-05-28-preparing-for-an-invasion/) — The Batman television craze hits Melbourne, as American promoter Alex Tolmer arrives to sell the 1960s TV phenomenon to Australian networks, with the show having already generated $5 million in royalties and 500 licensed Batman products from shaving cream to ice-cream.
- [The Great Football Fade-out](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-06-11-the-great-football-fade-out/) — A statistical and cultural argument that Melbourne's claim to be the world's greatest football city is overstated, with crowd figures failing to keep pace with population growth and a large section of the community only going through the motions of football devotion.
- [Everything in Apple-Pie Order](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-06-18-everything-in-apple-pie-order/) — A tour of Appletree Hill, a new outer-Melbourne housing estate designed entirely by architect Robin Boyd, where every house, garden, fence and toolshed follows his modernist principles, raising the question of whether living beautifully in Boyd's mould leaves room for a treehouse or a boat.
- [Flying Ladies and Rich Young Men](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-06-25-flying-ladies-and-rich-young-men/) — The eighth National Rally of the Rolls-Royce Owners' Club descends on Canberra with 101 cars, from pristine 1909 Silver Ghosts to the latest Silver Shadow, and Keith Dunstan discovers why collectors who already own four or five see no reason to stop.
- [Another Encore for the Square Dance](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-07-02-another-encore-for-the-square-dance/) — Melbourne's 110-year obsession with building a civic square is traced through a parade of proposals, from an 1856 newspaper leader and a Jubilee scheme tied to Parliament House, through post-war plans to demolish the Windsor Hotel and Princess Theatre, to the current stand-off with the English Hammerson development group over the Swanston and Collins Streets corner site.
- [Hitting the Clubs on the Head](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-07-09-hitting-the-clubs-on-the-head/) — Melbourne's private clubs face a crisis following the end of six o'clock closing, with the Hardware Club, University Club, Royal Caledonian Club and Public Schools Club all shedding members or contemplating moves, while the Yorick Club debates whether to merge with the Savage Club or simply wind up, and the boom business shifts to a carpet-lined hotel in Hawthorn with a Breathalyser at the bar.
- [Moses and the Monash Red Sea](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-07-16-moses-and-the-monash-red-sea/) — Charlton Heston visits Melbourne on a U.S. State Department goodwill tour, plays exhibition tennis against Frank Sedgman at Grace Park as a Bethesda Hospital fund-raiser, and gives poetry readings at Monash University and other venues, finishing with Robert Frost's 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', which he had read on a TV memorial program two days after President Kennedy's assassination.
- [Swinging Little Englanders](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-07-23-swinging-little-englanders/) — Two young British debaters on a Commonwealth Relations Office universities tour argue that the twentieth century is a cultural catastrophe, pitching swinging London against American mass culture and Pop Art, while a Melbourne audience votes the motion down 200 to 71, reassured by a student's observations on the creative forces of Picasso, James Joyce and Henry Moore.
- [Among the Pasties](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-07-30-among-the-pasties/) — A tour of Sydney's King's Cross strip clubs, from the Pink Pussy Cat to the Crazy Horse, appraising the performers, the audiences and the bizarre economics of a world where a good stripper earns seventy pounds a week and can appear at three clubs a night.
- [Wanted, a Civic Symbol](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-08-06-wanted-a-civic-symbol/) — The case for Melbourne's proposed Lower Yarra bridge as the city's long-missing civic symbol, with a detailed comparison of its planned dimensions against the Sydney Harbour Bridge and a sidelight on the Rebecca Riots as a precedent for toll-gate fury.
- [Conquering the Impossible Cowlick](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-08-13-conquering-the-impossible-cowlick/) — A tour of Melbourne's male grooming revolution, from the Aramis fragrance counter at Georges to the new unisex hairdressing salons, as barber shops discover cologne, skin cream and the concept of the male toiletry barmaid.
- [A Beautiful Blending of Blues](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-08-20-a-beautiful-blending-of-blues/) — The launch of the Men's Fashion Council's Australian Fashion Express tour, a train fitted out to spread the gospel of conservative dressing through the four eastern states, reported from Spencer Street with a wary eye on the matching Paisley cufflinks.
- [Queuing for the Grand Final](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-08-27-queuing-for-the-grand-final/) — The annual ritual of camping outside the MCG for football grand final tickets, chronicling the culture of canvas-town camaraderie, the absurdity of the regulations banning it, and the irony of the queue moving from the ground to the clubs.
- [A Really Fantastic Queue](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-09-24-a-really-fantastic-queue/) — Dr Leon Mann of Melbourne University's Psychology Department analyses the behaviour of VFL grand final ticket queues, explaining why people stay past the point where they know they have no hope of getting in, through wish-fulfilment and wounded pride.
- [A Marvellous Auction Sale](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-10-01-a-marvellous-auction-sale/) — A charity auction for Melbourne's Cultural Centre raises funds through improbable lots — LBJ's hat, Patrick White's autographed plays, Dita Cobb's false eyelashes — while the centre itself remains mired in a naming dispute between 'National Gallery and Art Centre of Victoria' and the simpler 'Artorium'.
- [Melbourne Cup Winners: Horses or Hats?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/melbourne-cup-winners-horses-or-hats/) — A survey of the Melbourne Cup as spectacle as much as sport, from Jean Shrimpton's mini-skirted 1965 Derby appearance and the ritual of Cup Day toppers and fashion parades to the race's history, Carbine's 1890 record run, and Archer's 550-mile walk to Flemington in 1861.
- [It Never Rains in the Mallee](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-10-08-it-never-rains-in-the-mallee/) — The opening of Australia's first full-scale Folk Museum at Swan Hill, built around the restored paddlesteamer Gem and a growing collection of Mallee farming machinery, with Sir Henry Bolte presiding over a sodden ceremony that proved the museum's name something of a misnomer.
- [A Place for Mr. Whippy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-10-15-a-place-for-mr-whippy/) — Myer's new $18 million Northland shopping centre opens in Melbourne's north, drawing 150,000 people on its first Tuesday and prompting a tour of its air-conditioned malls, waterless plastic fountain, bistro, gallery paintings and a Mr. Whippy ice cream van finally given a respectable home.
