- [Where Is the Eye of Monique?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-10-22-where-is-the-eye-of-monique/) — The Bureau of Meteorology's system for naming cyclones, explained through the man responsible for choosing 100 female names every three years, with a history tracing the practice from Brisbane's cantankerous nineteenth-century meteorologist Clement Wragge to the 1966-67 season's lineup of Angela, Colette, Monique and Odette.
- [The Four Days of President Johnson in Australia](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-10-29-the-four-days-of-president-johnson-in-australia/) — An eyewitness account of Lyndon B. Johnson's 1966 Australian visit, riding in the White House Press Gallery motorcade from Canberra airport and observing a presidential performance that put Australian political oratory to shame, while demonstrators outside the Rex Hotel held signs and protesters tore up placards.
- [In the Wake of the Shrimp](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-11-05-in-the-wake-of-the-shrimp/) — The 1966 Melbourne Cup Fashions in the Field contest, which pitted Dupont's model Jean Shrimpton against Wool's Baroness Fiona Thyssen, and Dunstan's interview with the Baroness about her life as a newly separated working model.
- [Which City is in Front...?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-11-12-which-city-is-in-front/) — A survey of the Melbourne versus Sydney rivalry, examining competing newspaper claims about population growth, migration, new industries, building completions and personal income, prompted by the CIA-level precision with which LBJ's visit was split equally between the two cities.
- [Courage, Not to Stumble, Brother](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-11-19-courage-not-to-stumble-brother/) — The history of Victoria's beer monopoly under Carlton and United Breweries, and the arrival of the Courage Brewery of England with plans for a $11 million Melbourne plant, raising the question of whether hotelkeepers will dare switch allegiances.
- [Getting into Troubled Waters](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-11-26-getting-into-troubled-waters/) — The long history of the Victoria-South Australia border dispute, from the 1839 survey through successive High Court and Privy Council cases to the 1966 standoff over offshore oil rights, with Sir Henry Bolte threatening a blockade of Corio whisky and Melbourne Cup horses.
- [1966 and All That](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1966-and-all-that/) — A tongue-in-cheek review of 1966, the year of decimal currency, Robert Menzies' retirement and Harold Holt's spear-fishing bikini photographs, the Pentridge escape of Ronald Ryan, conscription protests, the mini-skirt, and Lyndon Johnson's visit to Australia.
- [One Must Take a Stand](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-12-03-one-must-take-a-stand/) — The Melbourne Cricket Ground's history from its elegant colonial origins to the current demolition of the Grey Smith Stand and the Snake Pit bar, as a new $2.5 million three-tier stand is built to lift capacity to 122,000 and outrace the VFL's competing stadium at Waverley.
- [The Ways of a Greyfriars Man](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-12-10-the-ways-of-a-greyfriars-man/) — The enduring appeal of Billy Bunter and the Greyfriars school fiction of Frank Richards, whose 1966 holiday annual and school prospectus revealed a world of fagging, tuck shops and earnest house rules still finding eager readers among a certain generation of Melbourne book buyers.
- [Lost a Dragon, Gained a Tower](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-12-17-lost-a-dragon-gained-a-tower/) — The demolition of the St. James building at the corner of Bourke and William Streets, and the AMP Society's plans for a 37-storey office tower on the site, designed by the San Francisco firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and destined to be Melbourne's tallest building, albeit twelve feet shorter than its Sydney counterpart.
- [In a State over Hanging](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-12-24-in-a-state-over-hanging/) — Victoria's troubled history with capital punishment, from the 1951 triple execution of Jean Lee, Norman Andrews and Robert Clayton to the 1962 Robert Peter Tait case, and the imminent hanging of Ronald Ryan for the murder of prison warder George Hodson, with Premier Sir Henry Bolte refusing all deputations or reprieve.
- [The End of a Pressure Group](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966-12-31-the-end-of-a-pressure-group/) — Melbourne's hydraulic lift system, sentenced to close on 31 December 1966 after a 1962 pipe burst and a successful compensation claim, is mourned in a farewell visit to the City Council power house in Spencer Street, where the superintendent evokes eighty years of hydraulic history from the wool presses at the docks to the Regent Theatre's rising organ console.
- [The Napoleon Solo Caper](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-01-07-the-napoleon-solo-caper/) — A lunch at the John Batman Motor Inn with Robert Vaughn, the American actor playing Napoleon Solo in "The Man from U.N.C.L.E.", who held court on Vietnam, Kennedy politics, and the impossibility of crossing from television to film.
- [Times Past at Lorne](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-01-28-times-past-at-lorne/) — A return visit to the Lorne holiday resort on Victoria's surf coast, comparing its genteel 1906 reputation with the folksingers, coffee lounges, and renovated Pacific Hotel of 1967, with a nostalgic glance across the bay at the superior tone claimed by Portsea.
- [Protesting as a Way of Life](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-02-04-protesting-as-a-way-of-life/) — An interview with David Nadel, Monash Labor Club president and organiser of the Anti-Ky demonstration, on how Melbourne's protest movement works, from the organisation of marches to the legal strategy of passive resistance.
- [A Rare and Beautiful Occasion](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-02-11-a-rare-and-beautiful-occasion/) — Keith Dunstan attends the 90th anniversary race meeting at Great Western, where champagne at sixpence a glass, spirited betting, a Fashions in the Field contest judged by a pin-up model, and a tour of Seppelts' underground cellars make a gloriously eccentric Victorian country race day.
- [Has Anyone Here Seen Kelly?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-02-18-has-anyone-here-seen-kelly/) — Melbourne's Lord Mayor launches a $10,000 fly-control quiz competition, prompting Keith Dunstan to revisit the city's long war against blowflies through the writings of William Kelly, whose 1853 account of Melbourne's plague of flies remains the most vivid on record.
- [Meeting a White Hunter from the N.T.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-02-25-meeting-a-white-hunter-from-the-nt/) — A profile of Allan Stewart, former Black Watch lieutenant turned safari camp operator at Nourlangie in Arnhem Land, who runs big-game hunting for clients including Stirling Moss and Reg Ansett while cohabiting with buffalo herds, crocodiles, and memories of thirty days in Fanny Bay gaol.
- [Selling us Short on Derby Day](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-03-04-selling-us-short-on-derby-day/) — A campaign for shorts as a legitimate Melbourne summer uniform, tracing the saga of a tram conductor suspended for reporting for duty in white shorts, the Tramways Union's failed push for cooler uniforms, and the eccentric history of the garment Australians gave to the world.
- [Where do we go for our Blue Ribbon Security?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-03-11-where-do-we-go-for-our-blue-ribbon-security/) — The Victoria Coffee Palace's decision to seek a liquor licence marks the end of Melbourne's last great temperance hotel, prompting a survey of the coffee palace movement's rise and fall from James Munro's 1880 crusade to stripping clubs, executive bus trips to Sydney, and the creeping normalisation of alcohol in the city.
- [This is a fine state to be in](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/batmans-melbourne-this-is-a-fine-state-to-be-in/) — A survey of the deteriorating relations between Victoria and New South Wales, arguing Melbourne's case for its rightful place in the international air network via the new Tullamarine airport.
- [Morley's Moomba: a king for all occasions](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-03-25-morleys-moomba-a-king-for-all-occasions/) — English actor Robert Morley reigns as King of Moomba, dispensing caustic one-liners about Melbourne's streets, Flinders Street Station, and marching girls while accompanying Queen Patsy Ann Earp through the Moomba procession and losing enthusiastically at the Bendigo races.
- [A detour to Rutherglen's festival](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-04-01-a-detour-to-rutherglens-festival/) — A report on the first Rutherglen Wine Festival, where 15 local vineyards discovered that the word "alcohol" could draw crowds from 200 miles away, complete with a wine auction, a float parade, a Saturday night barbecue dispensing wine from pluto taps, and the liquor laws getting in the way of Sunday fun.
- [Doing the right thing by Ned](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-04-08-doing-the-right-thing-by-ned/) — A report on a Kelly school held in Wangaratta by the Adult Education Centre, where historians Manning Clark, Weston Bate, and Ian Jones assembled to debate Ned Kelly's legal case, military ambitions, and the possibility of a posthumous pardon from Monash University.
- [Alas, poor Tivoli, I knew it well.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/alas-poor-tivoli-i-knew-it-well/) — A eulogy for Melbourne's fire-gutted Tivoli Theatre, tracing its history back to the 1850s diggers' Varieties Music Hall through Harry Rickard's opulent 1901 rebuild and its parade of stars from Marie Lloyd to Harry Houdini.
- [Taking the row out of rowing](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-04-22-taking-the-row-out-of-rowing/) — The centenary Head of the River race on the Barwon traces how school rowing went from a grand social occasion of flour bombs, dunked coxes, and triumphant theatre nights to a tightly regulated event policed by three foolscap pages of Scotch College instructions, with Scotch winning in 1967 just as they had in 1868.
- [The unending wars of the planesmen](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-04-29-the-unending-wars-of-the-planesmen/) — A blow-by-blow account of the rival publicity battles between TAA and Ansett-ANA over the simultaneous arrival of their first DC9 jets in Melbourne, a rerun of the 1964 Boeing 727 toss-and-tactics war, from competing tarmac ceremonies to a champagne press breakfast and a contest over which airline could claim the most historically travelled passenger.
- [Art on a pastoral binge: wine, food, and fantasy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-05-06-art-on-a-pastoral-binge-wine-food-and-fantasy/) — A tour of the gallery movement sweeping Victoria's provincial towns, from the Hamilton Shaw Collection to Ballarat's hotbed of Lindsays and the new Mildura Arts Centre, where the third Mildura Prize for Sculpture drew a washing-machine agitator with a Ford Thunderbird tail-light and a taxi driver who reckoned the winner was two giraffes mating.
- [Here's, perhaps, another place for a future village](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-05-13-heres-perhaps-another-place-for-a-future-village/) — The case for Westernport Bay as Melbourne's future industrial port, measuring the bay's natural advantages against Port Phillip's treacherous entrance and Corsair Rock, as BP's new Crib Point refinery, a coming Esso oil refinery, and John Lysaght's steel works promise to transform the area.
- [Here's, perhaps, another place for a future village](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/heres-perhaps-another-place-for-a-future-village/) — A case for Westernport Bay as Victoria's great industrial port of the future, tracing the historical accident that gave Melbourne Port Phillip over the far superior Westernport and surveying the refineries, steelworks and soaring land prices already transforming the Hastings shoreline.
- [Met any good, used football players lately?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-05-20-met-any-good-used-football-players-lately/) — A comic proposal to apply used-car-lot logic to the VFL's open transfer market, prompted by the $8000 purchase of Hawthorn full-forward Peter Hudson from New Norfolk and the collapse of the Coulter Law against buying and selling players.
- [Met any good, used football players lately?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/met-any-good-used-football-players-lately/) — A survey of the collapse of the Coulter Law's genteel fiction that footballers cannot be bought and sold, tracing the season's transfer fees from country leagues to the VFL and proposing a Used Footballer Lot along the Nepean Highway where buyers could inspect cartilages and check ear counts.
- [As conspicuous as a negro at a KKK picnic](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-05-27-as-conspicuous-as-a-negro-at-a-kkk-picnic/) — A report from the Melbourne concerts of Little Stevie Wonder, whose extraordinary stage presence reduced a 7,000-strong teenage crowd to mass hysteria while Keith Dunstan stood out rather conspicuously as the only adult male among the screaming fans.
- [As conspicuous as a negro at a KKK picnic](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/as-conspicuous-as-a-negro-at-a-kkk-picnic/) — Keith Dunstan reports on Little Stevie Wonder's Australian tour, tracing the pandemonium of 7000 fans at a Sydney concert where police, security men and ambulance officers struggled to contain girls aged 14 to 17 fainting, weeping and tearing at their own hair, and contrasting the hysteria with the singer's composed, almost supernatural stage presence.
- [The straightest furrow in the west](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-03-the-straightest-furrow-in-the-west/) — A dispatch from the World Ploughing Championships at Wangaratta, where 17 nations competed in tracksuits and Tyrolean hats for the most exquisitely turned third of an acre, amid the competing din of five demonstration chain-saws.
- [The straightest furrow in the west](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-straightest-furrow-in-the-west/) — A report on the World Ploughing Championships held near Wangaratta, where representatives of 17 nations in Olympic blazers competed over a third of an acre each, Keith Dunstan finding the contest as soporific as Test cricket but discovering an unexpected tension in the twiddle of tappets and the measurement of furrows with a ruler.
- [The last touch to the business of the soft sell](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-10-the-last-touch-to-the-business-of-the-soft-sell/) — A brochure from the Melbourne Crematorium at Fawkner prompts a history of cremation in Victoria, from the illicit 1895 beach bonfire at Sandringham to the slow respectability won by the Cremation Society through the 1920s.
- [The other Edinburgh (Part one of two parts)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-10-the-other-edinburgh-part-one/) — The centenary of Prince Alfred's 1867 Australian tour passes unremarked, prompting a retelling of the extraordinary colonial welcome he received in Melbourne, culminating in the disastrous Citizens' Free Banquet in Richmond Park where 60,000 descended on provisions for 10,000 and the wine flowed literally into the street.
- [For Wally Hoysted, the whips are well and truly out](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-17-for-wally-hoysted-the-whips-are-well-and-truly-out/) — A portrait of Walter Hoysted, the solitary Melbourne anti-flogging campaigner who parks a furniture van outside Flemington cataloguing the number of times each horse is struck, challenges jockeys to take 20 strokes on the bare back for charity, and has been to jail for his trouble.
- [The other Edinburgh (Part two of two parts)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-17-the-other-edinburgh-part-two/) — The second part of the centenary retelling of Prince Alfred's 1867 Australian tour: the shooting of the Duke at Clontarf by Henry O'Farrell, the wave of anti-Irish feeling it unleashed across the colonies, O'Farrell's trial and execution, and HMS Galatea's quiet departure.
- [A poser: what to do with a million dead marines?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-06-24-a-poser-what-to-do-with-a-million-dead-marines/) — The rise of the no-return bottle threatens the bottle-oh, the Methodist Boy Scouts and the garbage men's European holiday funds, as the Bottle Merchants' Association and the soft-drink makers go to war over who owns Australia's empties.
- [Psychedelic underpants give a man assurance](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-07-01-psychedelic-underpants-give-a-man-assurance/) — Frank Eidlitz opens Melbourne's first psychedelic discotheque, the Ginza in Little Bourke Street, with six projectors throwing swirling images across dancers and ceiling while Keith Dunstan reports feeling merely queasy.
- [By day the loafers, at night the scoundrels](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-07-15-by-day-the-loafers-at-night-the-scoundrels/) — A centenary tribute to Melbourne's General Post Office, tracing its nine-year construction from 1859, its grand opening on Victoria's separation day weekend, and the "Argus" reviewer who warned its colonnade would be a paradise for loafers by day and scoundrels by night.
- [The sporting way to get rid of those messy crowds](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-07-22-the-sporting-way-to-get-rid-of-those-messy-crowds/) — A satirical proposal to abolish live sporting crowds entirely, replacing spectators with television coverage and piped crowd noise, saving clubs the expense of grandstands and parking while converting sports grounds into landscaped parks.
- [It's a tough job now keeping up with the Joneses](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-07-29-its-a-tough-job-now-keeping-up-with-the-joneses/) — Melbourne detective Barry Jones becomes the father of quadruplets, prompting reflections on the fertility drug gonadatrophin, the contraceptive pill's impact on Australia's birth rate, and a colonial-era account of a Warrnambool woman who gave birth to sextuplets in 1841.
- [Even 'Rock-Fist Rogan' couldn't win this one](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-08-05-even-rock-fist-rogan-couldnt-win-this-one/) — A campaign to amalgamate Melbourne's suburban councils into a Greater Melbourne authority founders against entrenched local resistance, with even a figurative street fighter unable to land a blow on the city's fragmented municipal politics.
- [Apres le ski it's the Tyrolean mini-skirts](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-08-19-apres-le-ski-its-the-tyrolean-mini-skirts/) — A field report from Falls Creek, where Victoria's ski fields are reinventing themselves with carpetbag steaks, wine lists and Tyrolean-costumed waitresses in a bid to match the plush reputation of New South Wales resorts like Thredbo.
- [For men only, and everything so discreet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-08-26-for-men-only-and-everything-so-discreet/) — A visit to Melbourne's first executive men's hairdressing salon, where hairpieces, tinting, permanents and facials are dispensed with the utmost discretion to businessmen who would rather not be seen to care about their appearance.
- [Nothing like the good old Carlton love-ins](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-09-02-nothing-like-the-good-old-carlton-love-ins/) — Melbourne's first hippie 'love-in' at Carlton's Love Centre draws a correspondent who finds young innocents in hired antique uniforms, psychedelic music, and a brisk trade in Iron Cross medals and Bob Dylan posters, with the hippie movement's second-hand military chic its most surprising feature.
- [They're high, wide, handsome and available](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-09-09-theyre-high-wide-handsome-and-available/) — Melbourne's office building boom has produced towers with prestige address plaques and embarrassingly empty floors, as the city discovers it cannot breed white-collar workers fast enough to fill the marble palaces rising across the CBD.
- [Where there's a Pill there's a way to get Leslie to Wesley](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-09-16-where-theres-a-pill-theres-a-way-to-get-leslie-to-wesley/) — The centenary history of Wesley College, written by Geoffrey Blainey and others, offers a frank account of headmaster scandals, flogging controversies and the school's transition from fee-starved colonial beginnings to producing Menzies and Holt, prompted by a fifth-form boy's letter to the school magazine about hooliganism in the corridors.
- [Lady Luck's favors are a real lottery](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-09-23-lady-lucks-favors-are-a-real-lottery/) — Tattersall's raises its ticket price to 60 cents and lifts the first prize to $25,000 in a lottery war against Queensland and New South Wales, while the story of how the sweep was driven from state to state by moral outrage before finding refuge in Tasmania illuminates both the gambling instinct and the wowser tradition.
- [Talking Turkey and a little Gaelic about football](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-09-30-talking-turkey-and-a-little-gaelic-about-football/) — The MCG's spectacular new western stand, with its cantilever overhangs, beer reticulation system and a scoreboard 115 feet above street level, is completed just in time for the finals, while Ron Barassi prepares to take a team to Dublin despite a Gaelic Athletic Association rule book that threatens suspension for anyone who plays or even attends cricket.
- [Home bottling goes down the drain](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-10-07-home-bottling-goes-down-the-drain/) — A fond elegy for Melbourne's home wine-bottling culture, tracing the pleasures of bulk barrels, siphons and improvised cellars as rising wine prices and shrinking supply begin to kill the tradition off.
- [No more bed and board for our Cliveden set](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-10-14-no-more-bed-and-board-for-our-cliveden-set/) — A history of Cliveden Mansions in East Melbourne, the grand apartment hotel built in 1887 by Sir William Clarke, tracing its rise as a resort of the colonial gentry and its long decline into an era of plastic flowers and electric rooftop signs.
- [The risks of tending phlox by night](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-10-21-the-risks-of-tending-phlox-by-night/) — Melbourne's worst drought in recorded history brings severe water restrictions, prompting a flood of inventive conservation measures from readers and a warning from the Board of Works that 360 plain-clothes inspectors are watching for illegal sprinkler use.
- [PMG knocks the mystique out of S.E.2](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-11-04-pmg-knocks-the-mystique-out-of-s-e-2/) — South Yarra's surge as Melbourne's swingingest suburb at the expense of fading Toorak, whose grand estates have been subdivided away and whose prestige postal code S.E.2 has been wiped out by the Postmaster-General's switch to four-digit numbers.
- [A cry in agony: 'Save the parking meters!'](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-11-11-a-cry-in-agony-save-the-parking-meters/) — A visit to Surfers Paradise finds the beach half-rebuilt after the storm that threatened to topple Garfield Towers into the surf, the Progress Association's Meter Maids still feeding sixpences into parking meters, and the new Mayor Bruce Small opening rotary conventions in lion cages and conducting the Salvation Army Band as a man of quite extraordinary civic energy.
- [Some imported fillies just aren't stayers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-11-18-some-imported-fillies-just-arent-stayers/) — A wry account of the Melbourne Cup's "Fashions in the Field" contest, the VRC's escalating quest for celebrity imports, and the diplomatic furore when Princess Soraya of Persia scratched at the last minute due to a dispute over transport and rising times.
- [Nowhere for a refined person to hang his hat](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-11-25-nowhere-for-a-refined-person-to-hang-his-hat/) — A lament for Melbourne's vanishing grand hotels and coffee palaces, as the Palace Hotel and Menzies Hotel face demolition to make way for new office towers, depriving the city of the establishments where Trollope, Paderewski and Dame Nellie Melba once stayed.
- [What is hatching at the sign of the golden cockerel](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-12-02-what-is-hatching-at-the-sign-of-the-golden-cockerel/) — A behind-the-scenes look at the brewing battle about to reshape Victoria, as British Courage Brewery readies its new Broadmeadows plant to challenge Carlton and United Breweries' long monopoly, with lavish press lunches, masked taste tests, and talk of two-tap hotels.
- [Around the turn and straight into the red](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-12-09-around-the-turn-and-straight-into-the-red/) — A detailed account of the financial crisis gripping Victoria's major racing clubs, with the VRC carrying an overdraft of $849,000 and the VATC similarly stricken, and the fierce political battle over mid-week racing and the threatened closure of Cranbourne, Werribee and Yarra Glen.
- [The art of upmanship among the joggers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-12-16-the-art-of-upmanship-among-the-joggers/) — A sardonic guide to the jogging craze sweeping Melbourne, from the competitive fibbing about distances run to the precise art of wearing a suitably battered track-suit, as middle-aged men driven by coronary anxiety thrash themselves around Caulfield racetrack before dawn.
- [The war on want strides painfully ahead](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-12-23-the-war-on-want-strides-painfully-ahead/) — A vivid account of Melbourne's sponsored walk fundraising craze, culminating in the 20-mile "Walk Against Want" to Dandenong in which more than 1200 people, including Jim Cairns, Barry Jones and a woman in high heels, raised nearly $18,000 for community aid abroad while covering themselves in blisters.
- [The Ghost of the Princess](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/the-ghost-of-the-princess/) — Tells the story of Federici, the Princess Theatre's baritone ghost who collapsed and died on stage playing Mephistopheles in 1888, and the book launch that tried, and failed, to lure his spirit out with themed cocktails.
- [The Bikini, What Next?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/the-bikini-what-next/) — A history of Australia's long, losing battle to regulate what beachgoers wear and when they may swim, from the segregated sea baths and bathing machines of the 1890s and William Gocher's 1902 defiance of Manly's bathing laws to the 1968 furore over the bikini.
- [The Year of Anti-Football Protest](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/the-year-of-anti-football-protest/) — Keith Dunstan's account of founding the Anti-Football League in 1967 with Douglas Wilkie, from the badge sold for the Berry Street Babies Home to the posthumous Wilkie Medal awarded to Prime Minister Harold Holt for never once being seen at a match.
- [How to cheat at wine tastings](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-australian-gourmet/how-to-cheat-at-wine-tastings/) — A tongue-in-cheek guide to bluffing your way through a masked-bottle wine tasting, from reading cork brands and capsule colours to timing your "hint of crushed violets" line for maximum effect.
- [Beef Boom in Tombstone Territory](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/beef-boom-in-tombstone-territory/) — A tour of American-financed cattle stations on Cape York Peninsula, where Sir William Gunn's Gunn Rural Management and the King Ranch operation at Tully were fencing scrubmaster herds, breeding Brahmans and Santa Gertrudis, and bulldozing rainforest for legume pasture.
- [Walkabout Profile: Jean Battersby](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/walkabout-profile/) — A profile of Dr Jean Battersby, newly appointed Executive Director of the Australian Council for the Arts, on subsidising drama, ballet, opera and film, her Sorbonne years on a French government scholarship, and her rejection of the "bricks and concrete" test for judging cultural investment.
- [Summer Madness](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/summer-madness/) — A wry survey of Australia's overloaded summer beach culture, surfboards, caravans, and competitive Rosebud campsites, from Portsea and Palm Beach's Toorak-set glamour to Surfers Paradise's Miami-style tower blocks.
- [Melbourne v. Sydney: The Love-Hate Feud](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/readers-digest/melbourne-v-sydney-the-love-hate-feud/) — A Melbourne man's affectionate account of the long civic rivalry between Melbourne and Sydney, from Parliament's original seat in Melbourne to the competing airports, opera houses and sporting loyalties that kept the two cities in a state of permanent, mostly enjoyable mutual suspicion.
- [How to Enjoy Hot Christmases](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/readers-digest/how-to-enjoy-hot-christmases/) — A defence of the Australian habit of serving roast turkey and plum pudding in midsummer heat, tracing Keith Dunstan's own Melbourne Christmases from the 1880s boom-era house of his childhood to a flying doctor's Christmas at Mt Isa, an Antarctic station's six-bottle dinner, and a Barrier Reef yacht.
- [This street was made for walking](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/this-street-was-made-for-walking/) — A defence of the pedestrianised Swanston Walk against councillors pushing to reopen it to traffic, citing survey figures showing it as the busiest pedestrian corner in Melbourne and the return of retailers like Levi Strauss and Nike.
- [The happy thwack of cash on willow](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/the-happy-thwack-of-cash-on-willow/) — A meditation on cricket's transformation from a game of beautifully organised boredom, best enjoyed dozing at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, into a business fought over by players threatening strike action for a share of ballooning sponsorship money.
- [Harbor no grudge, it's better here; The bay and me](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/harbor-no-grudge-its-better-here/) — A Boxing Day case for Port Phillip Bay over its more celebrated rival, touring favourite spots from Sea Winds and Point Nepean to the Sorrento ferry and a flathead-fishing trip with mate Doug Crittenden.
- [Moombas and shakers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/moombas-and-shakers/) — A profile of the Wittingslow family, the fairground dynasty who have run Moomba's rides and sideshows since patriarch Tom Wittingslow started out guessing weights at Penny Land in 1932, and who now stage the festival itself.
- [A new clutch of ugly ducklings blots the cityscape](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/a-new-clutch-of-ugly-ducklings-blots-the-cityscape/) — A nomination round for Melbourne's ugliest sights, from the Foxtel and Optus advertising signs looming over the historic Young and Jackson's Hotel to the kitsch interior of the new Imax Theatre and the warring columns of 101 Collins Street.
- [On the right track at last](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/on-the-right-track-at-last/) — The Lilydale-Warburton Rail Trail opens along a disused line closed by Henry Bolte in 1964, part of a growing Victorian movement converting old railway corridors into 36 kilometres of bush trail free of motor vehicles.
- [Once a vision, now a site for sore eyes](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/once-a-vision-now-a-site-for-sore-eyes/) — The gutted, empty Southern Cross Hotel four years after the Nauru Government's redevelopment plans collapsed, and a look back at the lively Eastern Market it replaced in the 1960s, the market where C.J. Dennis's Sentimental Bloke first met Doreen.
- [After 500 kilometres, still the kings (and queens) of the road](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/after-500-kilometres-still-the-kings-and-queens-of-the-road/) — The 15th Great Victorian Bike Ride brings 2100 cyclists 500 kilometres from Wahgunyah to Melbourne, among them 83-year-old veteran Alan "Curly" Hartup and the ride's youngest finisher, nine-year-old Anna Clements.
- [Obituary: Richard Cudlipp](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/obituary-richard-cudlipp/) — An obituary for advertising executive Dick Cudlipp, who rose to managing director of George Patterson Bates in 1965, drove Carlton and United Breweries' campaign against the Courage Brewery, and later became a Western District cattle and vineyard grazier.
- [Joy of sport lost in a country that takes it far too seriously](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/joy-of-sport-lost-in-a-country-that-takes-it-far-too-seriously/) — Reflects on Australia's outsized reaction to the 2010-11 Ashes loss under Ricky Ponting, arguing the country has forgotten that sport, unlike genuine disasters such as Cyclone Tracy, is meant to be enjoyed regardless of the result.
- [Plagues be upon us, let's hope for no divine retribution](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/plagues-be-upon-us-lets-hope-for-no-divine-retribution/) — A mock-biblical catalogue of Melbourne's afflictions during a wet 2010, led by a possum population boom under the Wildlife Act, and running through cars, mobile phones, football and noisy restaurants via the ten plagues of Exodus.
- [It's crunch time for Melbourne: we need a congestion tax](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/its-crunch-time-for-melbourne-we-need-a-congestion-tax/) — Argues Melbourne should follow London and Stockholm in adopting a congestion tax to break the city's addiction to the motor car, citing Bicycle Victoria figures on the rising share of peak-hour commuter cyclists.
- [Swear fines a nonsense when invective is so ineffective](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/swear-fines-a-nonsense-when-invective-is-so-ineffective/) — Marks new Victorian on-the-spot fines for swearing by recalling editor Michael Davie's landmark 1979 decision to print an obscenity in The Age, and proposes Paul Keating chair an inquiry into supplying Australians with fresh invective.
- [All I know about ethics, I learned at sword-point](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/all-i-know-about-ethics-i-learned-at-sword-point/) — Recalls a career of manufactured tabloid outrage, from a fake letters-page furore over Myer's window mannequins to a night spent hiding in a wardrobe from a sword-wielding husband, prompted by reflecting on the collapse of the News of the World.
- [Once, footy dominated our lives. Now, things are much worse](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/once-footy-dominated-our-lives-now-things-are-much-worse/) — Surveys the exponential growth of Australian Football League saturation since Keith Dunstan and Douglas Wilkie founded the Anti-Football League in 1967, from a single Saturday afternoon competition to year-round coverage, gambling and coaching sackings.
- [Obituary: Walter Joseph Hauser](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/obituary-walter-joseph-hauser/) — An obituary for Walter Hauser, one of the touring Vienna Mozart Boys' Choir singers stranded in Melbourne by the outbreak of war in 1939, who was taken in by Archbishop Daniel Mannix and went on to a career as an industrial chemist and Keith Dunstan's regular bridge partner.
- [Oh, for the daily thud on my lawn](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-age/oh-for-the-daily-thud-on-my-lawn/) — A tribute to the ritual of reading a printed daily newspaper in bed each morning, tracing Keith Dunstan's own newspaper family history against the decades-long death toll of Melbourne mastheads and Rupert Murdoch's prediction that print itself would be gone by 2020.
